(CNN) -- An Austrian man who allegedly held his daughter as a sex slave for 24 years has been charged with murdering one of their children, prosecutors say. Josef Fritzl is accused of fathering seven children by his daughter during her 24-year captivity. Austrian State Prosecutor Gerhard Sedlacek told CNN Thursday that Josef Fritzl, 73, was charged with murder because one of the seven children died in infancy. The other six children survived. Fritzl, a retired electrician from Amstetten, 75 kilometers (46 miles) west of Vienna, was also charged with rape, incest, false imprisonment and slavery. The murder charge stems from the death of Fritzl's infant son, Michael Fritzl, who died from lack of medical care, the prosecutor said.  Watch as Fritzl is charged with murder » . "Although he realized how life-threatening M.F.'s situation was after being born, Josef F. did not call out for help," Sedlacek said, explaining the charge. The trial is expected to begin early in 2009 and if convicted of murder Fritzl could face 10 to 20 years in prison. Austria, like other European countries, has no death penalty. Prosecutors say psychiatric tests show that Fritzl is mentally fit to stand trial but Sedlacek has asked that Fritzl be confined to a "mental asylum." Fritzl kept the daughter and all but three of the children in a cellar beneath his home in Amstetten, Austria, west of Vienna, officials say. Three of the children lived upstairs in the home Fritzl shared with his wife and several of their own children. Fritzl has been in custody since the case came to light in April, sparking worldwide attention. He had explained Elizabeth's disappearance in 1984 by saying the 18-year-old girl had run away from home, a story backed up by letters he forced Elisabeth to write, including one that begged her parents not to look for her. When Elizabeth gained her freedom, she told police her father began sexually abusing her at age 11. On August 8, 1984 -- weeks before she was reported missing -- her father enticed her into the basement, where he drugged her, put her in handcuffs and locked her in a room, she told police. For the next 24 years, she was constantly raped by her father, resulting in seven children, she said, according to the police statement. Fritzl's daughter and her children have since been receiving counseling although doctors warn that they will take years to recover. Members of the Fritzl family will also be offered the chance to adopt new identities in an effort to help them lead normal lives, officials said. Psychiatrist Max Friedrich, who treated the abducted Austrian teenager Natascha Kampusch, estimated it would take "between five and eight years" for the children to recover from their experiences.

Prosecutors said psychiatric evaluations found Fritzl mentally fit to stand trial, but Sedlacek has requested that he be confined to a “mental asylum.”

Officials said Fritzl kept his daughter and all but three of the children in a cellar beneath his home in Amstetten. The other three children lived upstairs in the house Fritzl shared with his wife and several of their own children.

Fritzl has remained in custody since the case came to light in April, attracting worldwide attention.

He had explained Elisabeth’s disappearance in 1984 by claiming that the 18-year-old had run away from home. He supported the story with letters he forced her to write, including one in which she begged her parents not to search for her.

**Historical breaking-news draft — based on developments after Josef Fritzl’s 2008 indictment**

# Austrian man charged with murder, rape and enslavement in cellar case

**ST. PÖLTEN, Austria —** Austrian prosecutors have charged Josef Fritzl with murder and a series of other offenses over allegations that he imprisoned his daughter in a concealed cellar for 24 years, repeatedly raped her and fathered seven children with her.

The murder charge—the most serious count—relates to the death of one of the children shortly after birth. Prosecutors allege Fritzl failed to obtain medical help for the newborn boy, knowing that the lack of care could cause his death. The infant’s body was later burned in a furnace, according to investigators.

Fritzl, 73, also faces charges including rape, incest, enslavement, coercion and false imprisonment. If convicted of murder, he could receive a life sentence.

The case emerged in April 2008 after one of the imprisoned children became gravely ill and was taken to a hospital. Medical staff appealed for the child’s mother to come forward, eventually prompting authorities to uncover a hidden underground complex beneath Fritzl’s home in Amstetten, west of Vienna.

Investigators say Fritzl confined his daughter, Elisabeth, in the windowless rooms beginning in 1984, when she was 18. Authorities allege he controlled access through a concealed, electronically secured door and threatened his daughter and the children if they attempted to escape.

Seven children were born during the confinement, prosecutors say. One died in infancy. Three remained underground with their mother, while three others were taken upstairs and raised by Fritzl and his wife after he allegedly staged their abandonment and produced letters purportedly written by Elisabeth.

## Murder charge centers on newborn’s death

The murder allegation rests on the prosecution’s claim that Fritzl deliberately withheld medical assistance from the newborn, who suffered serious breathing problems.

Under Austrian law, a person may face a murder charge for knowingly failing to act when legally obligated to prevent a death. Prosecutors contend that Fritzl understood the child was in danger but refused to seek professional care because doing so could have exposed the cellar and the years of abuse.

The charge is expected to be one of the most closely contested issues at trial. Fritzl’s defense could argue that he did not intend the child to die or did not fully appreciate the seriousness of the infant’s condition.

## Psychiatric assessment finds him fit for trial

A court-appointed psychiatric assessment concluded that Fritzl was mentally fit to stand trial and could be held criminally responsible for his actions.

The evaluating psychiatrist reportedly found that he had a severe personality disorder but was not suffering from a mental illness that prevented him from understanding the nature or wrongfulness of the alleged offenses. That conclusion clears a major procedural hurdle and means the case can proceed in criminal court.

The assessment may nevertheless influence sentencing and any decision about whether Fritzl should be held in an ordinary prison or in a secure institution offering psychiatric treatment.

## Trial expected in 2009

Proceedings are expected to begin in St. Pölten in early 2009 and are likely to attract intense international attention. Much of the evidence involving Fritzl’s daughter and the surviving children may be presented behind closed doors to protect their identities and reduce further trauma.

Authorities are expected to rely on statements from Elisabeth, physical evidence from the cellar, birth and medical records, and Fritzl’s own accounts to investigators. Prosecutors have said the evidence documents decades of systematic control, sexual violence and isolation.

Fritzl has acknowledged imprisoning his daughter and fathering her children, according to authorities, but his position on the full indictment—including the murder allegation—will be central to the trial.

## Victims receiving long-term care

Elisabeth and the surviving children have been receiving medical and psychological treatment at a secure location. Officials have released few details, citing confidentiality and the family’s need for privacy.

Doctors have said their recovery will be a long-term process. Family members who lived underground must adjust to daylight, open spaces and ordinary social contact, while all of the survivors face the psychological consequences of prolonged captivity, abuse and family separation.

The children raised upstairs are also receiving support as they come to terms with the circumstances of their upbringing and reunite with relatives who had been hidden from them.

Authorities and medical staff have urged the media and public to avoid identifying or approaching the survivors. Their condition and treatment remain protected by medical privacy rules, and officials have stressed that recovery cannot be measured simply by physical health.

Fritzl is being held in custody pending trial. The charges remain allegations unless and until established in court.
